# hoehner-openai-warrant-affidavit-and-return
- **URL:** https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.med.68915/gov.uscourts.med.68915.1.1.pdf (affidavit, 17 pp.) and https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.med.68916/gov.uscourts.med.68916.3.0.pdf (warrant + return, 2 pp.); dockets https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/71527762/united-states-v-hoehner/ and https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/71526267/united-states-v-hoehner/ · **Accessed:** 2026-09-16 · **For:** v2→v3 response round, slice L
- **What it establishes:** PRIMARY. In re Search of Records Associated with OpenAI/ChatGPT Account Searches, No. 2:25-mj-00305-KFW (D. Me.). Affidavit of HSI SA Gregory D. Squire: the warrant "seeks records and information pertaining to two unique, specific prompts made to OpenAI’s 'ChatGPT' program by a SUSPECT USER and the unique responses generated by ChatGPT" (¶2); sought under 18 U.S.C. § 2703 (¶4). The suspect told the undercover agent about the Sherlock Holmes/Q prompt on April 18, 2025 (¶17) and pasted a ChatGPT response (Trump-style Y.M.C.A. poem) on April 29, 2025 without specifying the prompt (¶19). Preservation request under § 2703(f) on May 20, 2025 (¶20). At the time of the application the suspect was UNIDENTIFIED and the stated purpose was identification (¶¶21–22). Warrant issued by Magistrate Judge Karen Frink Wolf at 1:01 pm, Sep 12, 2025; to be executed by Sept 24; 30-day delayed notice. Return: executed 9/13/2025; inventory "1 Excel Spreadsheet" from OpenAI; return filed 10/17/25. Docket: criminal complaint (with a separate Squire affidavit) against Drew Matthew Hoehner filed Sep 26, 2025 (2:25-mj-00324-KFW); indictment (2 counts) Oct 1, 2025 (2:25-cr-00148); not-guilty plea Nov 6, 2025. So the sequence is: unidentified as of Sept 12 → OpenAI return Sept 13 → complaint naming Hoehner Sept 26. The complaint affidavit itself was not available on RECAP (could not open); what identified him is therefore known to me only through Forbes and Gizmodo's quotation of the complaint.
- **Key passages:**
  - Aff. ¶2: "Specifically, this warrant seeks records and information pertaining to two unique, specific prompts made to OpenAI’s “ChatGPT” program by a SUSPECT USER and the unique responses generated by ChatGPT."
  - Aff. ¶21: "To date, HSI agents have been unable to identify the SUSPECT USER. While anonymity is a common benefit gained by users utilizing the dark web, there is probable cause to believe that OpenAI may have information or other records in its possession, such as Internet Protocol (“IP”) addresses, that could assist HSI in identifying and locating the SUSPECT USER."
  - Aff. ¶22: the records sought "would present a method of identifying the SUSPECT USER who is engaged in the commission of the SUBJECT OFFENSES."
  - Aff. ¶20: "On May 20, 2025, agents submitted a preservation request under 18 U.S.C. § 2703(f) to OpenAI for records pertaining to the prompts and responses as outlined above. Agents received a reference number of OPENAI-332."
  - Warrant (Doc. 3, p. 1): "Date and time issued: 1:01 pm, Sep 12 2025"; return (p. 2): executed "9/13/2025", inventory "1 Excel Spreadsheet".
- **Reliability:** Primary court documents (text layer extracted locally). The affidavit is the government's sworn account at the time of application; it cannot speak to what happened after Sept 12.
- **Relevance to this project:** L1. Decisive for wording: the warrant was a genuine attempt to unmask a user from two prompts (so Gizmodo's "DHS has not asked OpenAI for any identifying information" is wrong against the affidavit), but no document I read shows that OpenAI's return is what identified him, and Forbes says it was not needed. Also useful to the essay's legibility thesis: a § 2703(f) preservation letter froze the record four months before the warrant.
